parent_refutation_summary: Core (tier 1, Emotional/Reflexive; psychMechanism = genetic fallacy / psychologizing the arguer / biographical reductionism): reducing a philosophical position to its biographical origin to imply that identifying the personal catalyst invalidates it. Parent moves: (a) genetic fallacy run across philosophy — if biographical reduction invalidated belief it would void Nietzsche (illness), Marx (poverty), Kierkegaard (broken engagement), each catalyst real and each irrelevant to truth-value; (b) pathologization-of-dissent — medicalizing a position one cannot refute (the Soviet 'sluggish schizophrenia' parallel: convert opposition into clinical illness so it can be 'treated' rather than answered); (c) the consent-irony closer — if the childhood WAS the catalyst, that childhood was itself imposed without consent, so the objection inadvertently proves the proxy-gamble point. Newton-counter (medium/short): a troubled childhood did not invalidate calculus; the burned child's observation about fire is not less valid for the burn. Sources: EFIList genetic-fallacy/biographical-reductionism, pathologization-of-dissent, consent-irony.

responses_archetypeVariants.defender: The biographical dodge is the most personal form the genetic fallacy takes: "you don't believe this, you're just wounded — bad parents made you this way." Concede the biography without flinching, because flinching is the tell and the honesty costs nothing: yes, many antinatalists did arrive through their own suffering, and they should say so plainly rather than perform a laboratory neutrality nobody actually has. How you reached a truth is not evidence against it. That is the fallacy named, and naming it is most of the work — but the defender slot earns its keep on what comes next, because the move is a bet the interlocutor cannot collect on. He needs the hidden premise that trauma distorts toward falsehood. It does not. The one thing a bad childhood reliably does is strip the optimism filter that comfortable lives keep installed — so the wounded arguer is not seeing falsely, he is seeing without the anaesthetic. The child who was burned is not a less reliable witness to fire; he is the more reliable one, and "you only flinch at the stove because it hurt you" is not a refutation, it is a confession that the speaker has been spared the lesson. Then spring the dilemma the dodge walks straight into. To explain an entire philosophy by the childhood, the interlocutor must concede the childhood was severe enough to generate a whole worldview of opposition — which means he has just granted that the suffering was real and formative, the exact magnitude the antinatalist is pointing at. He cannot hold both "your pain was trivial, get over it" and "your pain was foundational enough to explain everything you believe." Pick one. If formative, it is data, and the argument is its report. If trivial, it cannot be the cause, and the diagnosis collapses. There is no third setting on which the biography both explains the belief and discredits it.
